L22: # The Narrows
L23: 
L24: #### Are The Narrows open?
L25: 
L26: High water, forecasted rainfall, and other factors can affect whether The Narrows are open for hiking. Stop by a visitor center or cite2†check our current conditions page for active closures.
L27: #### Are The Narrows safe?
L28: 
L29: Flash floods can happen at any time, and your safety is your responsibility. cite3†Learn about flash floods, common injuries, and other risks before entering The Narrows.
L30: The National Weather Service (NWS) issues flash flood potential forecasts. Stop by a visitor center or cite4†check the NWS website for current forecasts†www.weather.gov .
L31: ### Highlights
L32: 
L33:   * cite5†What are The Narrows? L34:   * cite6†Where can I see The Narrows? L35:   * cite7†How high is the water? L36:   * cite8†When should I go? L37:   * cite9†What should I bring? L38:   * cite10†What are the risks? L39: ## What are The Narrows?
L40: 
L41: As the name implies, The Narrows is the narrowest section of Zion Canyon. This gorge, with walls 1000 feet tall and the river sometimes only 20-30 feet wide, is one of the most popular areas in Zion National Park.
L42: Watch the video below to get an overview of The Narrows, or use the Highlights section to jump to routes, seasons, or safety.   [Button: Embed]
L43: # Embed Video
L44: 
L45: <iframe title="Video Embed" src="https://www.nps.gov/media/video/embed.htm?id=294C8ECB-155D-451F-67C5AAED14BBAD01" width="480" height="306" frameborder="0" scrolling="auto" allowfullscreen></iframe> [Button: Close ] [Button: Copy ] Open Transcript
L46: ### Transcript
L47: Welcome to Zion National Park, my name is Jonathan. Zion is a popular National Park where visitors come to immerse themselves within the grandeur of the canyon’s cliffs, and to challenge themselves with one of our many scenic and adventurous hikes. One of our more popular hikes visitors come to enjoy is the unique Narrows, a hike in a canyon that in places is only 20-30 feet wide, and 2000 feet deep.
L48: However, unlike most hikes, taking on the Narrows means actually traveling upstream through the Virgin River on uneven, slippery, and rocky river boulders. Due to the risks of a hike like this, proper preparation is imperative, both for your safety and your enjoyment. Every hiker in The Narrows should have closed toed shoes, even just your regular hiking boots, and a walking stick.
L49: Although weather might be over 100 degrees the day of your hike, this narrow section of the canyon can stay considerably cooler, making non-cotton clothing, like polypropylene or wool, more ideal for its insulating benefits even while wet. When you are planning your trip into The Narrows, you should also be aware of the flash flood potential. Afternoon thundershowers are possible throughout the year and a potential hazard to those hiking in slot canyons like The Narrows.
L50: During these events the river can quickly turn into a torrent of powerful rushing water, doubling and tripling in volume. Stop by the visitor center and speak with a ranger to get the most up to date conditions and the flash flood potential. Remember, even when you are prepared and conditions seem optimal, things can change quickly. Being aware of any changes in water clarity and increased river flow can go a long way in protecting your life.
L51: Being prepared and aware will help ensure a hike that will undoubtedly create positive memories that will last a lifetime. But please, ensure this opportunity for others by remembering to use the restroom before the start of your trip and to plan on packing out all your trash, including even the tiniest of crumbs. These simple guidelines will ensure the enjoyment of these special places for not only you, but generations to come.
L52: Duration:
L53:     2 minutes, 22 seconds
L54: Find out what to expect and how to prepare for one of Zion’s most popular hikes with Park Ranger Jonathan Fortner.
L55: ## Where can I see The Narrows?
L56: 
L57: You can see the start of The Narrows by cite11†hiking along the paved Riverside Walk trail for 1 mile from the Temple of Sinawava (Shuttle Stop #9). If you wish to see more, you will be hiking in the Virgin River. This can involve wading upstream for just a few minutes, or it can be an all-day adventure.
L58: The two options for hiking The Narrows are listed below.
L59: #### cite12†Bottom-Up Hike from the Temple of Sinawava (no permit required)
L60: 
L61: Hiking in The Narrows upstream as far as Big Spring does not require a permit. Doing the hike this way allows you to see some of the most spectacular and narrowest parts of the canyon. You can hike in the river for an hour and have a great experience, or you can hike as far as Big Spring, a strenuous, ten-mile round trip, all-day adventure.
L62: #### cite13†16-Mile Through-Hike from Chamberlain's Ranch (Wilderness Permit required)
L63: 
L64: Permits are required for this 16-mile through-hike of the Virgin River Narrows from Chamberlain's Ranch to the Temple of Sinawava. Those who choose this option must arrange their own cite14†transportation to the Chamberlain's Ranch trailhead.
L65: When conditions allow, cite13†apply for permits online or from a Wilderness Ranger at a cite15†visitor center .
L66: 
L67: * * *
L68: ## How high is the water?
L69: 
L70: Water flow fluctuates greatly from year to year and day to day depending on many factors, such as rainfall and snowmelt. You can cite16†check the current river flow on the USGS website.†waterdata.usgs.gov L71: The flow is measured in cubic feet per second (CFS). Here is a general overview of how river levels affect The Narrows:
L72:   * <70 CFS: When the river is running below 70 CFS, walking is moderately difficult. There are knee-deep crossings on the slippery and uneven river bottom, with frequent pools up to waist-deep.
L73:   * 70-150 CFS: When the current goes above 70 CFS, walking against the current becomes challenging. Thigh-deep crossings are frequent, and pools can be chest-deep.
L74:   * >150 CFS: If the flow goes over 150 CFS, The Narrows will be closed to all travel.
L75: The Narrows also closes when a Flash Flood Warning is issued by the National Weather Service. The Narrows will remain closed for at least two hours after a warning is lifted.
L76: * * *
L77: ## When should I hike The Narrows?
L78: 
L79: ### Summer and Fall
L80: 
L81: Most people hike The Narrows in the summer and early fall when the water level drops and tends to be at its warmest. However, keep in mind that cite17†life-threatening flash floods are more frequent during the monsoon season.
L82: Fall brings more stable weather, but the days get shorter and the water temperature drops. cite18†Read more about Zion's Weather and Climate here .
L83: ### Winter and Spring
L84: 
L85: Winter and early spring commonly bring high water levels and cold water. The Narrows will be closed during the spring when snowmelt raises the river over 150 CFS.

L104: ## What should I wear or bring?
L105: Hiking in The Narrows is comparable to walking on wet bowling balls. Closed-toed shoes and a sturdy hiking stick are recommended for hiking on the slick, uneven rocks. Sandals, crocs, or bare feet are not appropriate and often result in twisted ankles or crushed toes.
L106: High canyon walls and cold water create cooler conditions than anywhere else in Zion Canyon, so bring seasonally appropriate layers. Quick-drying fabrics are best for preventing hypothermia.
L107: You should also bring food, water, first aid supplies, and other gear for your safety. cite19†Visit our Narrows safety page for a more complete list of equipment and clothing recommendations.
L108: * * *
L109: ## What are the risks?
L110: Flash floods, cyanobacteria exposure, slips, falls, hypothermia, and other hazards are always possible. Even on short trips, this hike can be challenging and risky.
L111: Ultimately, you are responsible for your own safety. Visit the Narrows Safety page below to learn how to plan ahead and prepare.   cite3†Narrows Safety cite20†Image: Rescuers with a patient The Narrows is a strenuous trail that requires proper planning and equipment. Learn about flash floods, cyanobacteria, and more. cite12†The Narrows from the Bottom Up cite21†Image: A group of hikers walk through ankle-deep, rushing water. Hiking upstream in The Narrows does not require a permit.
L112: However, the hike is challenging. Read up on how to have a safe and fun trip here. cite13†The Narrows from the Top Down cite22†Image: A shallow river flows across the rocky bottom of a narrow canyon. Hike 16 miles through The Narrows starting at Chamberlain's Ranch. This is a permitted hike through Zion Wilderness. cite23†Narrows Regulations cite24†Image: Visitors with a map Know how to keep yourself safe and keep the Narrows wild and beautiful.

L20: cite1†Acadia National Park L21: # Nature
L22: 
L23: On This Page
L24:   Acadia National Park preserves approximately 50,000 acres along the mid-section of the Maine coast, containing the tallest mountains on the eastern seaboard, an iconic rocky Maine coastline, and subalpine rocky summits. The park’s cite2†mountains , cite3†lakes , cite4†streams , cite5†wetlands , cite6†forests , meadows, and cite7†coastlines contribute to the diversity of cite8†plants and cite9†animals found here.
L25: Acadia is within the transition zone between southern and northern forests, and as a result, hosts plant species and communities currently at the edge of their geographic range. The park’s location along the Atlantic flyway makes it an important resting and feeding place for migrating cite10†birds and cite11†bats .
L26: During your visit, you join a legacy of centuries of interconnectedness between cite12†people and this landscape . For more than 100 years, a tradition of cite13†scientific investigation has joined a millenium of cite14†traditional ecological knowledge to form the bedrock of our understanding of Acadia's natural world. Help protect Acadia's natural wonders by following all cite15†Leave No Trace principles during your visit and reducing your carbon footprint as you explore.
L27: * * *
L28: ## Animals: A Place Called Home
L29: cite9†Animals call Acadia 'home.' Their lives are inevitably wrapped up in ours as we move through the places they eat, sleep, and raise their young. Animals inhabit all of Acadia, from the smallest microorganism to the falcons and eagles that fly above the park's mountain peaks, and in every ecosystem in between. With a keen eye you can always be cite16†watching wildlife from a safe distance during your visit to Acadia.
L30: Simple acts like using long lenses when cite17†birdwatching can go a long way to keeping animals safe. Learn more about their remarkable lives and how you can protect Acadia's animals.   cite9†Animals Acadia is home to a diversity of wildlife, from microorganisms living in tidepools to larger animals on land and in water. cite18†Peregrine Falcons Learn more about how peregrine falcons, the fastest animal on earth, came back from the brink of extinction.
L31: cite11†Bats These small, often misunderstood animals lead incredible lives. Learn about them and the many threats that have pushed them to brink. cite19†Loons Learn about the remarkable lives of the loons that dot the lakes and ponds of Acadia. cite20†Amphibians and Reptiles Frogs, snakes, turtles, and salamanders species in Acadia. cite21†Invertebrates Learn about invertebrates in the air, on land, and beneath the water. cite22†Fish Inhabitants of Acadia's many lakes, ponds, and streams.
L32: * * *
L33: ## Plants: The Green Kingdom
L34: There are over 1,000 different types of plants in Acadia. As generations of humans cite23†worked these woodlands and cite24†waters and waterfronts , plants formed the foundation of their survival. On land, low-to-the-ground plants such as mosses, grasses, ferns, and lie beneath larger plants such as trees and shrubs. Joining these plants on the ground are lichens and mushrooms which are not true plants, but organisms that are unique in the natural world.
L35: In tidepools, saltmarshes, and on the coast, marine algae, seaweed, and other saltwater plants rise and fall with the tides. You can visit the cite25†Wild Gardens of Acadia for an up-close look at native plants or join a ranger for one of our many cite26†guided walks .   cite8†Plants The diversity of Acadia National Park is reflected in its plant life; more than 1,100 plant species are found here. cite27†Freshwater Plants†nps.gov Life abounds in the serene waters of Acadia’s lakes, ponds, and streams.
L36: From waterfowl to fish, wildlife depends on aquatic vegetation. cite28†Saltwater Plants and Marine Algae Learn more about the remarkable life of plants that thrive in Acadia's saltwater environments including tidepools. cite29†Conifers: Evergreen Trees and Shurbs Cone bearing plants with dark green, needle like leaves are a prominent feature of the Acadia landscape. cite30†Mosses Get a close up look at this class of plants that carpet moist areas such as rocks, trees, and along stream beds.
L37: cite31†Lichen Not quite a plant, not just a fungus, learn more about these unique organisms that paints so much of Acadia's landscape. cite32†Mushrooms & Other Fungi Driving all the biodiversity we see above ground, from the trees to wildflowers, is an underground web of fungal life.
L38: * * *
L39: ## Ecosystems: From Summit to Sea
L40: Taken all together, the land and sea and the plant and animal life form unique natural environments called cite33†ecosystems . Along with cite34†geologic features like glacial erratics and cobblestone beaches, these ecosystems are Acadia. It is a place forged in the fire of ancient volcanoes and carved by ice. Acadia is rarely flat ground, from the sculpted granite mountains with summits and cliffs to the glacially-scoured lake beds and stream valleys.
L41: At the base of the mountains, the land is dotted with wetlands or continues it slope down to rocky headlands that have been undergoing a ongoing assault by the weather and the sea since their formation.   cite2†Mountains Acadia is home to more than 20 mountains that rise from the sea and comprise much of Mount Desert Island. cite7†Coasts and Rocky Shorelines Acadia protects nearly 64 miles of coastline on Mount Desert Island, Schoodic Peninsula, Isle au Haut, and other islands.
L42: cite6†Forests Acadia is blanketed with forests and woodlands that are situated in the transition zone of two ecoregions. cite3†Lakes and Ponds Lakes and ponds add shimmering contrast to Acadia's forested and rocky landscape. cite4†Streams and Watersheds Learn about the running waters that provide life to wildlife, plants, and humans in Acadia National Park. cite5†Wetlands, Marshes and Swamps All classes of wetlands (swamps, marshes, and bogs) are found within the park.
L43: * * *
L44: ## Enjoy the View: Night Skies and Scenic Views
L45: Acadia possesses remarkably cite35†dark skies for its proximity to Portland, Boston, and New York. The Milky Way dazzles visitors and reminds us just how large our “home” galaxy truly is. When the moon is full, the light it reflects from the sun is so bright it can cast a glow across the ocean. During the day, both the cite36†motor road system and the (non-motorized) cite37†carriage road system at the park were carefully laid out by prominent landscape architects to take advantage of spectacular cite38†views .
L46: From the top of the mountains or on one of the park's many cite39†historic hiking trails , enjoying the view is one of the key experiences in Acadia. Both of these incredible Acadia visual experiences are constantly under threat from light pollution and air pollution. Learn more about what can do to protect the view.   cite38†Scenic Views and Viewsheds Learn about the natural and historically designed scenic views in Acadia as the lengths scientists are going to to protect them.
L47: cite40†Acadia's Night Skies†nps.gov Acadia National Park possesses remarkably dark skies for its proximity to Portland, Boston, and New York.
L48: * * *
L49: ## Environmental Threats
L50: cite41†Climate change is rapidly changing Acadia's environment. Rising temperatures, warming waters, rising seas, and extreme weather events are increasing environmental stress leaving plants, animals, and ecosystems more suceptable to damage, as well as cite42†pests and disease . Among the greatest environmental challenges facing Acadia National Park is the presence and threat of invasive species.
L51: Non-native species, especially those considered cite43†invasive plants or invasive animals, threaten communities of native plants and animals across the United States. Located along the mid-coast of Maine, Acadia is downwind from large urban and industrial areas in states to the south and west. Periodically, high concentrations of cite44†air pollutants blow into the park from these areas and create hazy views and unsafe breathing conditions.
L52: Coupled with overtourism, the environment of Acadia is threatened on various fronts. Federally threatened or endangered species are on the tip of the spear. You can help protect Acadia during your visit by following all posted signs and regulations, riding the cite45†Island Explorer or carpooling, and following cite46†Leave No Trace principles. Learn more about the cite47†environmental theats that face Acadia National Park.
L53:   cite41†Climate Change As national parks and green spaces everywhere experience large scale climate change, what do we stand to lose? cite43†Invasive Plants Invasive plants threaten Acadia's native ones. Learn more about these alien invaders and the steps park staff take to keep them at bay. cite44†Air Pollution and Visibility Acadia is deeply involved in the National Park Service's comprehensive air resources management program.
L54: cite48†Threatened & Endangered Species Learn more about the federally and state listed endangered and threatened species managed by Acadia National Park.
L55: * * *
L56: ## How Does It Work?: Natural Processes and Concepts
L57: Behind the beauty of Acadia is a fascinating sets of processes at work. The cite49†geologic history of Acadia National Park stretches back in time through millions of years to the formation of the oldest rocks on Mount Desert Island and continues to the present with the persistent forces of wind and weather which cause erosion. Evidence of this rich geologic past can be seen across the island, along rocky shorelines and atop windswept mountains. The cite50†tides shape Acadia on their twice daily rise and fall.
L58: cite51†Wildland fire has shaped the cite52†natural disturbance of the plants and animals of Acadia from the earliest lightning strike to more recent human activity for agriculture and fire prevention. The result of all these processes at work is an Acadia that is rich in cite53†biodiversity - the collective plant, animal, and microbiotic world.
L59:   cite49†Geology Acadia's landscape tells the tale of a time when fire and ice covered these lands. cite50†Tides The twice daily tides is caused by the gravitation pull of the moon. Learn more about this fascinating natural process. cite53†Biodiversity Learn about the abundance of life at Acadia known as biodiversity. cite52†Natural Disturbances Learn how fire, weather, water, earthquakes and other natural disturbances dramatically change the landscape.
L60: cite51†Wildland Fire The fire management program at Acadia National Park performs a full range of wildland fire management operations and services. cite54†Erosion: Wind, Water & Weather Learn about the soft and hard forces that over time erode the Acadia landscape including wind, water, and weather

L20: cite1†Joshua Tree National Park L21: # Nature
L22: cite2†Wildlife cite3†Image: a large lizard sunning itself on a rock What animals might you see on your Joshua Tree visit? How do they thrive in the desert environment? cite4†Plants cite5†Image: many wildflowers scattered across the desert soil The original name proposed for Joshua Tree was "Desert Plants National Park." The desert is home to an impressive number of plant species.
L23: cite6†Natural Features & Ecosystems cite7†Image: landscape with many Joshua trees and rounded rock formations Why does this striking landscape look the way it does? Find out how powerful geologic forces have sculpted the land. cite8†Environmental Factors cite9†Image: a fallen Joshua tree showing blackened burn marks from a past fire More fires, declining air quality, disturbed lands, invasive species, light pollution: these are some of the challenges facing the park.
L24: cite10†Climate Change cite11†Image: Large granite boulder piles backlit by a setting sun. Learn how climate change is affecting Joshua Tree National Park and what we are doing to mitigate its effects.   Joshua Tree’s nearly 800,000 acres were set aside to protect the unique assembly of natural resources brought together by the junction of three of California’s ecosystems:
L25:   * The Colorado Desert, a western extension of the vast Sonoran Desert, occupies the southern and eastern parts of the park. It is characterized by stands of spike-like ocotillo plants and “jumping” cholla cactus.
L26:   * The southern boundary of the Mojave Desert reaches across the northern part of the park. It is the habitat of the park’s namesake: the cite12†Joshua tree . Extensive stands of this peculiar looking plant are found in the western half of the park.
L27:   * Joshua Tree’s third ecosystem is located in the westernmost part of the park above 4,000 feet (1,219 m). The Little San Bernardino Mountains provide habitat for a community of California juniper and pinyon pine.
L28: The plant diversity of these three ecosystems is matched by the animal diversity, including healthy herds of desert bighorn and six species of rattlesnakes. Joshua Tree National Park lies within the Pacific flyway for migratory cite13†birds , and is a rest stop for many. It was for this unusual diversity of plants and animals that Joshua Tree National Monument was set aside on August 10, 1936. The park also encompasses some of the most interesting cite14†geologic features found in California’s desert areas.
L29: Exposed granite monoliths and rugged canyons testify to the tectonic and erosional forces that shaped this land. Washes, playas, alluvial fans, bajadas, desert varnish, and igneous and metamorphic rocks interact to form a pattern of stark beauty and ever-changing complexity.
